newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Slash Australia textile, shoe tariffs, agency urges.
newsitem.headline: Slash Australia textile, shoe tariffs, agency urges.

text.p: Australia faces a fresh row over industry protection after the country's key industry adviser on Monday urged textile clothing and footwear tariffs be slashed to five percent by 2008.
Three weeks after the government slowed cuts in car tariffs in the face of industry opposition and chronic unemployment, its Industry Commission warned against stalling further reforms.

The Commission, in its draft report on the textile, clothing and footwear (TCF) sector, said current tariffs of up to 37 percent cost Australians A$1.94 billion (US$1.44 billion) in 1996/97, held back living standards, eroded economic growth and failed to protect jobs.

"Ultimately, the losses to the Australian economy as a whole have been borne in lower living standards for everyone, but the losses to those whose businesses have failed or whose jobs have disappeared are more severe," the commission said.
The textile, clothing and footwear industry, along with car manufacturing, are Australia's last remaining sectors enjoying high trade protection.
Under an existing programme, TCF tariffs will be cut to 25 percent for clothing and about 15 percent for footwear and textiles by 2000, compared with general tariffs of about five percent by 2000.
The commission recommended further gradual cuts in TCF tariffs to a uniform five percent by July, 2008, with no pause in reductions and no further review of protection.
It warned the conservative Liberal-National government against stalling on tariff cuts for the sector.
"The argument that further stalling tariff reductions should await significant progress on microeconomic reform is superficially appealing, but without foundation," it said.
The commission will consult industry, union and other groups before preparing a final report for the government in September.

But Australia, until recently a leading force in the international push for free trade, has shown an increasing reluctance to make unilateral cuts in trade barriers, discouraged by slow reforms elswhere and troubled by unemployment approaching nine percent.
Prime Minister John Howard this month rejected similar urgings by a similar agency, the Productivity Commission, to slash car tariffs.

Faced with industry warnings of lost jobs and investment, Howard opted to freeze car tariffs at 15 percent until 2005, when they would be cut to 10 percent. The commission had recommended car tariffs be cut to five percent by 2005.
But he said Australia remained committed to an ambitious regional pact to axe trade barriers early in the next century.

The Industry Commission said its plan for the TCF industry would see about five percent of the sector's 96,000 jobs go, but added this would be more than offset by more jobs in retailing and other industries currently hit by the high TCF protection.
It recommended assistance for displaced workers, regions hit hardest by the reforms and a A$10 million textile development fund.
Treasurer Peter Costello said the government would respond "in due course" after the commission's final report.

High unemployment and a perception that Australia has cut its own trade barriers too quickly while other countries lag behind has eroded political support for tariff cuts among the major political parties.

But Canberra remains bound by the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum's free trade pact that commits its members to abolishing all trade barriers -- by 2010 for developed nations such as Australia and 2020 for developing countries.
